- Can you confirm the exact contractual incident-notification timeline Redwood is proposing for confirmed personal-data incidents that affect Acme users? Our InfoSec team wants to see a clear maximum (we’re currently tracking 48 vs. 72 hours options).
- We need to know what evidence Redwood can provide on request (logs, packet captures, KV cache snapshots) and any limitations (redaction, proprietary code).
- Please confirm whether Redwood will provide a one-time export of the full subprocessor list for Acme (including regions / last-onboarded date). We will need an export for our EU transfer impact assessment.

We attached a short list of DPA questions (Acme_DPA_questions.pdf).

Elaine —

Thanks for the clear list. Quick answers up front, then proposed next steps below:

1) Notification timeline (contract language we propose): 
   - "Initial customer notification": Redwood will provide an initial notice to Customer as soon as reasonably practicable after Redwood confirms a security incident affecting Customer personal data, and in any event no later than 72 hours after Redwood’s confirmation.
   - "Follow-up report": Redwood will deliver a targeted follow-up report (scope, affected data categories, mitigation steps) within five (5) business days of confirmation, with additional updates as material facts change.

   Rationale: GDPR supervisory-notification is 72 hours; Redwood will commit to internal triage to reduce customer-facing lag where possible, but we need the contractual "no later than" window to align with legal/forensics workflows and cross-team evidence collection.

2) Evidence & redaction:
   - Redwood can provide logs, event timelines, and aggregated KV-cache metadata relevant to the incident. Raw internal debug traces and source-code level logs may be redacted to remove privileged operational material.
   - When evidence contains Customer PII of non-impacted third parties or Redwood internal identifiers, Redwood will produce a redacted export and document the redaction rationale.

3) Subprocessor export:
   - We can produce a one-time export (CSV) of our current subprocessor roster including region, primary role, and date onboarded. We will also flag subprocessors that process data in APAC/EU.
   - Turnaround: 3 business days after agreement on the recipient contact and execution of a short data-reception acknowledgement.

Next steps I propose:
- I’ll attach our internal incident-notification runbook as a reference (see attached redwood-incident-process.pdf).
- Neha, could you confirm language tolerance on the 72-hour "no later than" vs. a 48-hour hard window?
- Elaine / Morgan & Blythe: let us know who should sign the acknowledgment and whether you require a DocuSign link for the subprocessor export.

Happy to hop on a 30-min call next week to go through example redactions and evidence formats.

Thanks,
Logan Wright

Elaine / Logan / Marissa —

Quick legal perspective to supplement Logan’s proposal. Quoting Logan below for context.

> "Initial customer notification: Redwood will provide an initial notice ... no later than 72 hours after Redwood’s confirmation."

Two important points for drafting the clause:
1) Statutory timeframe: Under GDPR Art. 33 the controller (customer) has 72 hours to notify the supervisory authority after becoming aware of a personal-data breach; processors (Redwood) typically commit to notify the controller without undue delay. Because timelines can depend on verification, our recommended contract language is: "Redwood shall notify Customer without undue delay and, where feasible, provide initial notification within forty-eight (48) hours of confirmation; in any event Redwood shall use commercially reasonable efforts to provide initial notification no later than seventy-two (72) hours after confirmation." This hybrid approach offers operational realism while acknowledging regulatory expectations.

2) Evidence scope and privilege: We should be explicit that Redwood will provide forensic timelines and relevant logs but reserves the right to redact or withhold internal privileged material. Recommended language snippet: "Redwood will provide such incident-related evidence as is reasonably required by Customer to comply with applicable data breach notification laws, subject to reasonable redaction for Redwood privileged information and to protect the security of other Customers."

3) Subprocessor export/process: We can provide the export under a short data-reception acknowledgement. For cross-border transfer questions, we will indicate whether SCCs or equivalent transfer mechanisms are in place for any subprocessor handling EU/UK data, and provide contact for our Privacy & Compliance team for deeper discussions.

I’ll prepare a redline that follows the hybrid 48/72 language and include the suggested evidence/redaction paragraph. If Acme insists on a 48-hour contractual hard cap, we should note an exception for complex multi-subprocessor incidents where additional triage is required — otherwise we risk promising an operational SLA we can’t meet across all cases.

- We request a one-time subprocessor export (CSV) including: name, service role, country, contact, date onboarded, and whether SCCs / adequacy / other transfer mechanism apply.

- Cross-border transfers: if Redwood relies on SCCs between Redwood and any subprocessor, please flag that in the export. Otherwise provide an explanation of the legal basis for transfer.

We have prepared a recipient form for the export; please respond if Redwood requires any execution. We are aiming for the export and the draft redline by EOD Thursday (18 Mar).
